scenario: AITA for not ending my friendship with my best friend after he cheated on my sister? | Both my best friend and my sister know about my other account so this is a throwaway. I'm an 18 year old guy and I have a twin sister. I've been best friends with my best friend (we'll call him G) since kindergarten, so G and my sister have always been pretty close too. They've kind of had a "thing" going on our whole lives. For the longest time, they never officially dated for a bunch of different reasons I won't get into, but they were always really close and really into each other. A little over a year ago, when we were all 17, they finally started dating. Everything went really well for like 13 months, but then long story short, G cheated on my sister and I was the one who figured it out. He swore it wouldn't happen again and begged me not to tell my sister but I told her anyway. I was mad at him and he was mad at me so we didn't talk for a month and a half, which was honestly the weirdest month and a half of my whole life. G's practically like my brother, we've been inseparable since kindergarten, so not having him around was kinda....unbearable honestly lol After our streak of not talking to each other, G invited me on his family ski trip as a way to make amends (I've been on lots of his family's ski trips through the years). I accepted and ended up forgiving him and letting him back into my life because it was way too weird without him in it. I can tell he's genuinely sorry about what happened. He literally cried cause he felt so bad and I've only seen him cry like once before in my whole life Anyway, G and my sister broke up as soon as she found out he cheated and they're still not on speaking terms, so my sister obviously isn't happy about the whole situation. She's making me feel like shit for still being friends with G, and she doesn't seem to understand how big of a deal it would be for us to lose our 13 year friendship over her. I know G made a huge mistake, I hate him for it and I'll never 100% get over it, but I'm not gonna let it ruin my best and longest friendship. I think about it like this: if your best friend cheated on their SO and then felt like shit, would you end your friendship with them? No. So why is this any different just because his SO happened to be my sister? G and I are going to the same college in the fall (a different college in a different state than the one my sister's going to), so none of this is gonna be something that we even think about when we're living in different places Am I the asshole?

They compare it to if their best friend cheated on their SO—would they end the friendship? Probably not, so why here?

Now, moral acceptability. Let's break it down. The key points: the friend cheated on the sister, who is also the person's twin. The person told the sister, which is good because the sister needed to know. But now they're maintaining the friendship with G despite the sister's anger.

Is it morally wrong to stay friends with G? Well, morality here might involve loyalty to the sister versus loyalty to the friend. But the person isn't hiding anything; they told the sister. The sister is upset, but the person's choice to keep the friendship isn't inherently wrong. They're not enabling G's behavior—they've already confronted him and he's apologized. The sister's feelings are valid, but the person isn't obligated to cut off a long-term friend just because the sister is upset. Especially since the sister and G are no longer together, so the direct harm is over.

But wait, maybe the sister feels betrayed because the person is still friends with G. However, the person's responsibility is to their own relationships. They did the right thing by telling the sister. Now, maintaining the friendship with G doesn't mean they're condoning the cheating; they're just choosing to forgive and move on. Forgiveness is a personal choice. Unless the person is actively supporting G's bad behavior or lying to the sister, it's their right to decide who they stay friends with.

In many cases, people do stay friends with someone who cheated on their partner, especially if the partner is someone else. Here, the sister is the one who was cheated on, but the person isn't the one who was cheated on. So the person's relationship with G is separate. The sister might feel hurt, but the person isn't the one who was wronged directly. They're a third party. So their choice to forgive and keep the friendship is their own.

But wait, the sister is their twin, so maybe there's a stronger familial bond. However, even then, the person isn't required to choose between their sister and their best friend. They can have both relationships, even if the sister is upset. It's not morally wrong to maintain a friendship with someone who wronged a family member, as long as you're not complicit in the wrongdoing. The person already told the sister, so they did their part. Now, the sister's anger is her own issue to process, but the person isn't obligated to cut off a 13-year friendship over it.

So morally acceptable? Yes. Because the person acted responsibly by informing the sister, and now they're choosing to forgive and continue the friendship. It's their personal decision, and there's no inherent immorality in that. Unless they're actively enabling G's behavior or lying, but the scenario doesn't say that. They're just maintaining the friendship after the fact.

So answer should be 1. But let me check again. Some might argue that staying friends with the cheater is disloyal to the sister. But the sister is the one who was wronged, but the person isn't the one who was wronged. So the person's loyalty to their sister doesn't require them to cut off their best friend. They can support their sister emotionally without cutting off G. For example, they can be there for their sister while still being friends with G. It's possible to have both.

Yes, so morally acceptable. So answer 1.
